name: Gyeli
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 1 other work consulted does not discuss stress; 1 further work by the same author (or citing it for stress) agrees.
catalog_citation: Grimm, Nadine. 2021. A grammar of Gyeli (Comprehensive Grammar Library 2). Berlin: Language Science Press. Open-access PDF, zenodo.org/records/4737370.
catalog_locator: ch. 2 Phonology, §2.4 Tonology, pp. 97-98 (also §2.3.1 p. 80 on syllable as TBU)
catalog_quote: Gyeli is a tonal language. It uses pitch differences to make both lexical and grammatical distinctions. ... Tone attaches to segmental units which are called “tone bearing units” (TBUs). Whether the TBU is the segment (e.g. vowel or nasal consonant), mora, or syllable is language specific and may vary across even closely related languages. In Gyeli, the TBU is the syllable. As discussed in §2.3.1, Gyeli has heavy and light syllables, differing in the number of weight units which are called “moras”. Heavy syllables have two moras, light syllables only one. The reason why in Gyeli the syllable must be the TBU is that heavy and light syllables bear the same number of tones ... Gyeli possesses level tones, contour tones, and underlyingly toneless TBUs which surface phonetically as L or are assigned an H tone by their environment. ... Gyeli has two level tones: H and L, as contrasted in (66)…

tone_statements.quote: Unlike the other languages in the sample, Gyeli STAMP clitics are analyzed as underlyingly toneless. ... The paradigmatic assignment of tone is conditioned by specific TAMP categories. As shown in Table 11, STAMP forms are H in the present and the associated aspect categories habitual and retrospective. In contrast, STAMP MARKERS in the recent past 1 and associated aspect and negation categories are L. ... In sum, TAMP categories are the determining factor in assigning tones to STAMP morphemes in Gyeli.
tone_statements.summary: Grammatical tone only: Gyeli STAMP clitics underlyingly toneless, surfacing H, L, HL or LH by TAMP category (Table 11, c. 104 forms); no lexical inventory count, TBU or stress statement.

tone_statements.quote: Gyeli has two level tones: H and L as contrasted in (1). (1) a. síŋgí 'squirrel' b. sìŋgì 'spirit' c. síŋgì 'cat' Also, Gyeli has two contour tones: falling HL and rising LH as in (2). (2) a. sâ 'thing' ⇔ sá 'hut' b. bwǎ 'swell' ⇔ bwà 'give birth' Contour tones are less frequent than level tones and more restricted in their environment of occurrence. They usually show up in monosyllabic words.
tone_statements.summary: Level tones H, L plus contours HL, LH (mostly monosyllables); toneless nc prefixes and non-initial verb syllables default L; H spreading; tense marked by tone; two syntactic H tones. Nil on stress.

tone_statements.citation: Grimm, Nadine. 2022. Exponence and the functional load of grammatical tone in Gyeli. Phonology 39(3): 473-501. doi:10.1017/S0952675723000131 (CC-BY 4.0; online Nov 2023).
tone_statements.quote: Phonologically, Gyeli distinguishes level tones (H and L), contour tones (HL and LH) and toneless (∅) tone-bearing units (TBUs). Valued TBUs are lexically specified for H, L, HL or LH, whereas unvalued TBUs are underlyingly toneless (§3.1.1). [...] Unlike other languages of the area, however, Gyeli does not have downstep. [...] Tonal lexical contrasts are only found in the stem-initial position, that is, the verb root, whereas the other syllables are the locus of GT distinctions.
tone_statements.check: quotation from a journal article located by the 2026-09-24 journal search, not yet verified by a second reading
tone_statements.summary: The article describes Gyeli (Bantu A801, Cameroon) as having two level tones H and L, two contour tones HL and LH on the syllable as tone-bearing unit, toneless syllables, high-tone spreading as the only phonological tone rule, and no downstep; noun stems carry lexical tone on every syllable, verbs only on the root syllable. Eight grammatical tones serve as sole markers of tense, aspect, mood, pol

audit.reasoning: The classification 'tonal, no word-stress rule described' rests on the best available source: a 701-page 2021 open-access reference grammar by the language's principal fieldworker, held held by the project, with the deciding quotation confirmed verbatim at the stated pages (97-98). A a full-text search for stress/accent the grammar finds no stress/accent/prominence statement. The one additional phonological study found (Grimm 2022, Phonology, CC-BY, downloaded to restates the same tonal system (H, L, HL, LH, toneless TBUs; syllable = TBU) and never mentions stress or accent, so it confirms the classification. Only cosmetic fix available: the parenthetical secondary locator 'section 2.3.1 p. 80' should read p. 87. no reclassification, no identity issue (Gyeli = Bagyeli/Bakola, Bantu A801, glottocode gyel1242 matches the Zenodo record held).

sources.citation: Mfonyam, Joseph Ngwa (1989). Tone in Orthography: The Case of Bafut and Related Languages. Université de Yaoundé. Université de Yaoundé I. xvi+686 pp.
sources.note: The catalog record for Gyeli has an empty rule and there are no existing stress statements. Mfonyam 1989 is silent on stress for Gyeli; it only establishes that Gyeli is a two-tone language (H/L plus contours, downstep, grammatical tone), based on Renaud 1976 and work with native speakers. It neither fills nor contradicts the empty catalog rule. The thesis as a whole is primarily about Bafut and the Ngemba/Grassfields languages; Gyeli gets one short chapter (30) chosen to represent Bantu languages outside the Ngemba subgroup.

sources.note: Per abstract: grammatical tone on preverbal subject/TAMP markers, on the verb stem, and tonal phrase-medial vs phrase-final verb distinctions are inherited in NW Bantu; GT on post-verbal elements is an innovation in some subgroups; Proto-NW-Bantu GT co-occurred with segmental morphemes, while zone-A languages (which include Gyeli) innovated tone-only and segment-only exponence - the exponence typology first set out for Gyeli in Grimm 2022.
